terminal.description: A shell in your workspace. The demo runs each task in turn and prints what it gives back right away and after await.

tasks.title: Wait with await
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 1` in `src/checkout.js`, make `paidLine(order)` charge `order.totalCents` with `chargeCard` and give back a promise of one line: the order id, then ` paid, code ` and the code on the receipt, like `'WC-3001 paid, code A-118'`. The lesson shows how to write it with `async` and `await`.

Check calls `paidLine` with orders of its own and answers the card machine itself.
nextSteps: Wait for the receipt with `await chargeCard(...)` and keep it in a `const`.
Return the line made from the order and the receipt, and run the demo.
hints: `chargeCard` gives back a promise of the receipt. The receipt's `code` is only there once that promise is fulfilled.
`await` in front of the call gives you the receipt itself, and `await` needs `async` in front of the function around it.
The body has the shape `const receipt = await chargeCard(order.totalCents)`, then `return` the line with `order.id` and `receipt.code` in it.

tasks.title: Always a promise
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 2`, make `stockFor(name, noted)` give back a promise of the count of the candle called `name`. `noted` is an object of counts Theo wrote down today, like `{ Fig: 0, Sage: 9 }`. When `name` is in `noted`, the count comes from there and the stock room is not asked. Otherwise it comes from `countStock`.

Either way, `stockFor` gives back a promise. Check calls it with notes of its own, a noted count of `0` included, and looks at whether the stock room was asked.
nextSteps: Read the lesson's part on what an async function gives back.
Ask whether `name` is in `noted`, the way the issue on objects showed.
If it is, return the noted count. If not, return the count from `countStock`.
Run the demo: both lines of Task 2 show a promise right away.
hints: Whichever way it goes, the caller gets a promise. An `async` function always gives back a promise, even when it returns a value it already had.
A count of `0` counts as false, so `if (noted[name])` asks the stock room about it. Ask whether the property is there at all instead.
The body has the shape `if (name in noted) { return noted[name] }`, then `return await countStock(name)`, inside an `async` function.

tasks.title: Count, then decide
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 3`, make `reorder(name, target)` count the candle called `name` with `countStock`. When there are at least `target`, it gives back a promise of `'Cedar: enough in stock'` for Cedar. Otherwise it orders as many as are missing, `target` minus the count, with `orderCandles`, and gives back a promise of a line made from the delivery: `'Cedar: 6 ordered, arrives Thursday'`.

Check answers the stock room and the supplier itself, and looks at what the supplier was asked for and when.
nextSteps: Read the lesson's parts on forgetting `await` and on deciding after a wait.
Wait for the count, then compare it with `target`.
When there are enough, return the first line.
Otherwise wait for the delivery from `orderCandles` and return the line made from it.
hints: Two machines, one after the other, with a decision between them. Each needs its own `await`.
Without `await`, the count is a promise: in a sum it gives `NaN`, and it is never at least `target`. Without `await` on the order, the delivery's `count` and `arrives` are `undefined`.
The shape is `const count = await countStock(name)`, then an `if` that returns the first line, then `const delivery = await orderCandles(name, target - count)` and the second line.

tasks.title: Close a sale
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 4`, make `closeSale(order)` charge the order, with your `paidLine` from Task 1 for example, and once it is paid, and not before, take `order.qty` candles of `order.candle` from stock with `takeFromStock`. It gives back a promise of a list of two lines: the line from `paidLine`, and `'Sage: 7 left'` when 7 sage candles are left.

Check answers the card machine and the stock room itself, and looks at whether the candles were taken only after the card machine answered.
nextSteps: Read the end of the lesson's part on what an async function gives back.
Then wait for what `takeFromStock` says is left.
Return a list of the two lines, and run the demo.
hints: `paidLine` is an `async` function, so it gives back a promise. Treat it like any machine of the shop.
Without `await` on `paidLine`, the list holds a promise, and the candles leave the shelf before the card machine has answered.
The shape is `const paid = await paidLine(order)`, then `const left = await takeFromStock(order.candle, order.qty)`, then `return [paid, ...]`.
